# 5. Terminology {#sec-terminology}

Every term this document defines, in one place, grouped by the register it belongs to: the two structural devices first, then pressures and levers, restorative functions, archetypes, and last the field vocabulary the lexicon adopts from elsewhere and pins down. Each entry gives the short definition and links to the section that develops it. The [alphabetical index](index-alphabetical.qmd) is the same set ordered A–Z, for when you know the word but not where it lives.

Many of these terms name something you could point to on a site. This plate anchors those across the two scales at which they act — the parcel and the array.

![The lexicon's spatial vocabulary anchored across two scales: a parcel-scale plan (siting-led restoration) and an array-scale section (structure- and management-led restoration), with the footprint as the shared anchor between them. Structure terms are drawn in charcoal; the five [restorative functions](4-restorative-functions.qmd) appear in colour at their physical homes. The conceptual naming terms defined below — agrisolar, ecovoltaics, dual use, LER — have no single element to point to.](../figures/fig_terminology_scales.svg){#fig-terminology}

### 5.1 Scale {#sec-terms-scale}

Developed in [§1, The Scale Transect](1-the-scale-transect.qmd).

#### Scale Transect {#term-scale-transect}

A single gradient from farmstead (A1) to regional (A5) that most other terms are read against, defined by covarying attribute bundles rather than capacity thresholds. See [§1](1-the-scale-transect.qmd).

#### Covarying attribute bundle {#term-covarying-bundle}

The set of attributes — interconnection, decision unit, permitting, management mode, capital, community interface, siting latitude — that move together along the transect, so naming a zone tells you many things at once. Nameplate capacity is an indicator, not a definition. See [§1.1](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-transect-why).

#### A0 — the zero-land case {#term-a0}

Arrays mounted on buildings, which take no ground at all: no siting latitude to spend, no ground layer to design, and no [sharing–sparing position](#term-sharing-sparing) to hold. It sits at the transect's origin rather than on it. See [§1.2](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones).

#### A1 — Farmstead {#term-a1}

<100 kW, under about an acre; behind-the-meter, single owner-operator, existing farm labour and equipment. See [§1.2](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones).

#### A2 — Field {#term-a2}

100 kW–1 MW, roughly 0.5–8 acres; behind-meter to distribution, landowner with possibly one lease counterparty. See [§1.2](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones).

#### A3 — Parcel {#term-a3}

1–10 MW, roughly 5–80 acres; distribution, community solar or mid-market PPA, multi-party, purpose-built ground management. The widest part of the [feasible wedge](#term-feasible-wedge). See [§1.2](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones).

#### A4 — Landscape {#term-a4}

10–50 MW, roughly 60–400 acres; developer-led institutional capital, contract-enterprise ground management. See [§1.2](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones).

#### A5 — Regional {#term-a5}

50 MW+, from roughly 300 acres to 10,000 and beyond; transmission, utility or IPP across jurisdictions, contract enterprise at ranch scale. Open-ended by design. See [§1.2](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones).

#### Siting latitude {#term-siting-latitude}

The designer's freedom over where the array goes. What governs it migrates from opportunistic placement to land assembly and grid topology up the transect, and it peaks at A2–A3 — bounded by the parcel at A1 and by the land market at A5. The constraint that makes the feasible region a [wedge](#term-feasible-wedge). See [§1.4](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-siting-latitude).

#### Restoration mode {#term-restoration-mode}

Whether restorative work is delivered by choice of ground, by array geometry, or by operation. The mode shifts as siting latitude falls up the transect. See [§1.4](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-siting-latitude).

#### Siting-led {#term-siting-led}

Restoration mode in which the restorative work is done by the choice of ground; requires A2–A3 latitude. See [§1.4](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-siting-latitude).

#### Structure-led {#term-structure-led}

Restoration mode in which array geometry is the instrument: clearance, row spacing, module transmissivity. See [§1.4](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-siting-latitude).

#### Management-led {#term-management-led}

Restoration mode in which placement is a given and the ground cover, grazing regime, and operational schedule carry everything. The dominant mode at A4–A5. See [§1.4](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-siting-latitude).

#### Stocking density {#term-stocking-density}

Instantaneous animals per unit area at a moment; diverges from carrying capacity with forage growth, utilization, and climate. A grazing design variable to calibrate, not a fixed rate. See [§1.3](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-grazing).

#### Carrying capacity {#term-carrying-capacity}

The season-long forage the land sustains over time, distinct from instantaneous [stocking density](#term-stocking-density). See [§1.3](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-grazing).

#### Contract grazing {#term-contract-grazing}

Grazing delivered as a contracted vegetation-management service by a party who does not live on site; appears at A3 and scales up into a logistics enterprise. See [§1.3](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-grazing).

### 5.2 Sharing and sparing {#sec-terms-sharing}

Developed in [§2, The Sharing–Sparing Axis](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd).

#### Sharing–Sparing Axis {#term-sharing-sparing}

The second, largely scale-independent dimension: whether the array shares land with agricultural production, spares land by taking ground out of it, or neither. Five positions, centred on S3. See [§2](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd).

#### S1 — Full sharing {#term-s1}

Production continues within the array footprint, in the same ground — vegetable [agrivoltaics](#term-agrivoltaics), crops between rows. See [§2.1](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions).

#### S2 — Functional sharing {#term-s2}

The ground layer is productive but subordinate to the array — grazing, forage. Available at every scale, and with S3 the spine of the [feasible wedge](#term-feasible-wedge). See [§2.1](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions).

#### S3 — Coexistence {#term-s3}

Neither sharing nor sparing: the array takes ordinary ground outright and the revenue sustains the farm enterprise holding it, so the restoration is socioeconomic before it is biophysical. The centre of the axis, and where most projects sit. See [§2.1](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions).

#### S4 — Idled-land sparing {#term-s4}

The array occupies ground already idle, marginal, or out of production, so that productive land is spared; the benefit accrues to the land *not* taken. See [§2.1](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions).

#### S5 — Impaired-land retirement {#term-s5}

Production ends on ground that carried a measurable off-site burden — chronically low yields, high runoff, nutrient or pesticide export, irrigation draw beyond the aquifer's budget — or on ground positioned where that burden can be intercepted. The removal acts on the ground taken itself. See [§2.1](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions).

#### Bare conversion {#term-bare-conversion}

Ordinary ground converted with the farm operation ended: the same ground fact as S3 without the restorative one. The non-restorative baseline the axis is read against, not a position on it. See [§2.1](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions).

#### Reading rule {#term-reading-rule}

Production first, then prior status. A site where production continues within the footprint is S1–S2 whatever the ground used to be; only where production stops do S3–S5 apply, told apart by what the ground was beforehand. See [§2.1](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions).

#### Feasible wedge {#term-feasible-wedge}

The feasible region across scale and sharing, shaped like a lens: all five positions open at A3, closing toward the S2–S3 middle at both extremes — at A5 as land assembly and capital discipline remove the poles, at A1 as in-footprint farming and meaningful sparing both need more scale to be real. Each thinned corner has a documented exception. See [§2.2](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-wedge).

### 5.3 Pressures and levers {#sec-terms-pressures}

Developed in [§3, Design Pressures](3-design-pressures.qmd).

#### Design pressures {#term-design-pressures}

The competing forces every site must resolve. Unlike axes they have direction, they conflict, and real parties advocate for them. Eight are named. See [§3.1](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures).

#### Generation yield {#term-generation-yield}

Pressure: maximize energy per unit land. Pulls toward dense row spacing, optimal tilt and tracking, low clearance, whole-field coverage. See [§3.1](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures).

#### Capital discipline {#term-capital-discipline}

Pressure: minimize installed cost per watt. Pulls toward standard racking, low clearance, minimal ground preparation, conventional geometry. See [§3.1](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures).

#### Operational simplicity {#term-operational-simplicity}

Pressure: minimize management burden across a 25–40 year asset life. Pulls toward uniform, mowable or gravel ground cover — and can oppose capital discipline, since native seeding raises capex and lowers long-run opex. See [§3.1](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures).

#### Agricultural continuity {#term-agricultural-continuity}

Pressure: keep working land working. Pulls toward high clearance, equipment access, production [ground layers](#term-ground-layer), farmer contracts. See [§3.1](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures).

#### Restorative ambition {#term-restorative-ambition}

Pressure: make ecological, hydrological, and economic resilience a design objective co-equal with generation. The pressure this document exists to advance — and still a force among forces. See [§3.1](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures).

#### Social license {#term-social-license}

Pressure: secure and sustain community acceptance *and* community benefit — two forces that can come apart, held under one name because they have to be advanced together. See [§3.1](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures).

#### Offtake conformity {#term-offtake-conformity}

Pressure: satisfy whoever is buying the power, the attributes, or the tax position. The channel through which outside parties push their requirements onto a design. See [§3.1](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures).

#### Decommissioning & reversibility {#term-decommissioning-pressure}

Pressure: minimize the residual footprint left after a 25–40 year asset life and preserve the option to return the ground to its prior use. For the end-of-life vocabulary itself, see [Decommissioning / Repowering / Reversibility](#term-decommissioning). See [§3.1](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures).

#### Pressure conflict {#term-pressure-conflict}

The framing that treats disputes between pressures — agricultural continuity vs. restorative ambition, operational simplicity vs. everything — as legitimate forces in genuine tension rather than as definitional errors. See [§3.2](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-conflicts).

#### Design levers {#term-design-levers}

The adjustable choices a designer uses to settle the pressures, in three families — structural, land-and-ecology, institutional — kept separable so each can be extended on its own. See [§3.3](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-levers).

#### Levers × Scale-Zones matrix {#term-lever-matrix}

The descriptive grid of how each lever's latitude and character shift across zones A1–A5, recording what is typical and available rather than what is required. See [§3.4](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-lever-matrix).

### 5.4 Restorative functions {#sec-terms-functions}

Developed in [§4, Restorative Functions](4-restorative-functions.qmd).

#### Restorative function {#term-restorative-function}

A restorative capacity a project can be designed to deliver, obtainable to varying degrees from many structural positions at once; a *column* of the [archetype × function matrix](#term-archetype-function-matrix). Four are biophysical, one socioeconomic. See [§4](4-restorative-functions.qmd).

#### Hydrologic function {#term-fn-hydrologic}

The site water balance as a design objective: infiltration and recharge raised, runoff slowed and filtered, soil moisture buffered — and, at scale, consumptive use retired from a basin's water budget. See [§4.1](4-restorative-functions.qmd#sec-fn-hydrologic).

#### Soil & carbon function {#term-fn-soil}

Perennial, low-disturbance cover rebuilding soil organic carbon and aggregate stability under and between the panels, against a construction-disturbance debt paid first. See [§4.2](4-restorative-functions.qmd#sec-fn-soil).

#### Biodiversity & habitat function {#term-fn-biodiversity}

Habitat built from the ground layer up — floral resources, nesting substrate, and vegetation structure — with mowing and grazing *timing* as decisive as the seed mix. Reachable across S2–S5, which is why it is a function and not a position. See [§4.3](4-restorative-functions.qmd#sec-fn-biodiversity).

#### Microclimate & thermal–water buffering function {#term-fn-microclimate}

The array's reshaping of the near-surface energy balance: lower daytime temperature and vapour-pressure deficit, higher nighttime minima. Its sign flips with climate and crop. See [§4.4](4-restorative-functions.qmd#sec-fn-microclimate).

#### Community & economic function {#term-fn-community}

The one socioeconomic function: the economic prosperity, livability, and health and equity a project builds for its host — the [SCALE](#term-scale-footprint) Communities domain read as an outcome, and distinct from the [social-license](#term-social-license) pressure and [community-benefit](#term-community-benefit) lever that aim at it. Only legible once the recipients are named separately. See [§4.5](4-restorative-functions.qmd#sec-fn-community).

#### SCALE footprint {#term-scale-footprint}

A whole-project reading across four domains — Sustainable Communities, Agriculture, Landscapes, Energy — each running from regeneration to depletion. Evaluative by design, but carrying direction rather than a pass mark. See [§4](4-restorative-functions.qmd#sec-scale).

#### Structure register / function register {#term-registers}

The document's two layers: the *structure* register is the scale × sharing–sparing axes and the [archetypes](#term-archetype) they produce; the *function* register is the restorative capacities laid over them. See [§4](4-restorative-functions.qmd).

#### Archetype × function matrix {#term-archetype-function-matrix}

The descriptive model relating the two registers: archetypes as rows, functions as columns, each cell the degree to which an archetype makes a function reachable. A palette, not a scorecard; the fully scored grid is deliberately not attempted. See [§4](4-restorative-functions.qmd).

### 5.5 Archetypes {#sec-terms-archetypes}

Developed in [§6, Archetypes](6-archetypes.qmd).

#### Archetype {#term-archetype}

A recurring way the [design pressures](#term-design-pressures) have been resolved at a particular scale zone and sharing position, carrying particular functions. Used in its plain sense — a characteristic, transformable pattern, not an exhaustive set. See [§6](6-archetypes.qmd).

#### Featured archetype {#term-featured-archetype}

One of the six archetypes developed in depth, in scale order: Barnyard Shelter Solar, Vegetable Agrivoltaics, Marginal Land Solar, Solar Prairie Strips, Regenerative Solar Grazing, Water-Sustainability Solar. Each recurs in the field and carries at least one documented case. A curatorial label, not a claim that these six are more valid than the [further archetypes](6-archetypes.qmd#sec-further-types). See [§6](6-archetypes.qmd#sec-featured).

#### Overhead and interspace systems {#term-overhead-interspace}

The engineering standards' hardware typology (DIN SPEC 91434; the NREL / InSPIRE configuration taxonomy): *overhead* systems mount modules above the working surface, *interspace* systems mount them low with the crop or cover between the rows. It classifies the structure, where an archetype classifies the resolution of pressures. See [§6](6-archetypes.qmd).

### 5.6 Regionality {#sec-terms-regionality}

Developed in [§7, Regionality](7-regionality.qmd).

#### Regionality {#term-regionality}

The claim that the [design pressures](#term-design-pressures) resolve differently in different places, because the factors that weight them vary across space. The vocabulary is constant everywhere; which positions are available, which functions are reachable, and how hard each pressure pulls are not. See [§7](7-regionality.qmd).

#### Regional factors {#term-regional-factors}

The six spatial factors the lexicon reads a region by: the **resource** (sun and cloud, including diffuse fraction), the **grid operator** (queue, curtailment, and the state programs that decide whether A3 exists), **aridity** (which flips the sign of the shade effect), **latitude** (which sets tilt, row spacing, and the inter-row light budget), the **cropping system** (which decides whether sharing is conceivable), and **irrigation** (which makes retirement at scale available or unavailable). See [§7.1](7-regionality.qmd#sec-rg-factors).

#### Regional calibration {#term-regional-calibration}

A restatement of the lexicon's indicative values for a particular region — capacity bands, absent zones, the binding constraint, the positions realistically open. The US calibration in §7.2 is one such, not the general case; calibrations from other regions are additions rather than corrections. See [§7.2](7-regionality.qmd#sec-rg-us).

#### Design import {#term-design-import}

The characteristic regional failure: carrying a resolution from the region where it was demonstrated into one whose factors differ — a shade benefit shown in the Southwest assumed in the Midwest, a habitat specification calibrated on one establishment cost written into a contract for another. [Offtake conformity](#term-offtake-conformity) is the usual vehicle, since a buyer's criterion travels further and faster than the evidence behind it. See [§7.3](7-regionality.qmd#sec-rg-consequences).

#### Diffuse fraction {#term-diffuse-fraction}

The share of irradiance arriving as diffuse rather than direct-beam light. Cloud collapses the beam component while diffuse holds up, so humid and cloudy regions run a higher diffuse fraction — light that is non-directional, reaches under and between panels, and is most of what a [ground layer](#term-ground-layer) lives on. It also weakens the case for tracking. See [§7.1](7-regionality.qmd#sec-rg-resource).

### 5.7 Field terms and metrics {#sec-terms-field}

The vocabulary the lexicon adopts from the wider field and pins down for use here.

#### Agroenergy {#term-agroenergy}

Energy infrastructure sited and designed to interact intentionally with agricultural or ecological land function. Umbrella term, not solar-specific.

*Term collision, flagged deliberately.* Elsewhere "agroenergy" (and *agro-energy*) most often means agriculture-*derived* **bioenergy** — energy crops, crop residue, biogas, biomass — i.e. farmland as a fuel source. This lexicon repurposes the word for the converse: energy *infrastructure* placed on and integrated with agricultural land. The reuse is intentional but worth naming, so a reader arriving from the bioenergy literature is not misled.

#### Agrisolar {#term-agrisolar}

Agroenergy specific to photovoltaics — the lexicon's working umbrella, because it is neutral across the [sharing–sparing axis](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd). The word is already in active use — NCAT's DOE-funded **AgriSolar Clearinghouse** promotes it for solar co-located with agriculture, and this lexicon draws case material from that body of work. Where the lexicon differs is in **broadening** the term past agricultural co-location: as used here *agrisolar* also covers the positions with no farming in the footprint at all (S3–S5), so the word names the whole design space rather than only its production end.

#### Agrivoltaics {#term-agrivoltaics}

Crop or livestock production within the array footprint (S1–S2). Terminology is regionally fractured: *agrophotovoltaics* in German literature, *agrivoltaics* in French and US usage, *photovoltaic agriculture* in Chinese literature, *solar sharing* in Japanese usage.

**Syn.:** agrophotovoltaics (German); photovoltaic agriculture (Chinese); solar sharing (Japanese).

#### Ecovoltaics {#term-ecovoltaics}

Solar development incorporating ecological understanding into array design *and management*, co-prioritizing ecosystem function with generation (an ecological ground layer, which this lexicon treats as a [restorative function](4-restorative-functions.qmd) rather than an axis position — most often built at S3). No universal definition exists, but the useful frameworks converge:

- @tolgyesi2023 offer five pillars: eco-smart landscape siting; eco-smart layout; trait-based design of novel grassland ecosystems; lifespan management; and stakeholder engagement embedded in a viable business model. **Pillars 4 and 5 treat management and business model as design questions, not afterthoughts.**
- @walston2025 characterize ecovoltaic development as sited on previously disturbed land, co-prioritizing generation with restoration — with measured outcomes, including more grassland bird species and more stable communities than row-crop controls.
- The literature makes **operational** claims, not just planting ones: an ecovoltaic approach to array operation might orient panels parallel to the sun's rays in the morning to maximize light reaching plants — a tracking-schedule decision.

> **The definitional dispute.** AFT advances a production-based definition of dual use; critics argue it excludes ecosystem benefits and imposes a one-size-fits-all instrument on farmland protection. Both terms are defined precisely above, and both map to positions on the [sharing–sparing axis](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions) — which locates the disagreement where it belongs, as a genuine conflict between agricultural continuity and restorative ambition (§3.2) rather than as a misuse of words. This document describes that dispute; it does not adjudicate it.

**Source:** @sturchio2023 — [Sources](sources.qmd).

#### Dual Use {#term-dual-use}

A production-based term: co-location that keeps *active agricultural production* within the array footprint across the project's life — American Farmland Trust's criterion. Structurally a mandate for [S1–S2](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions). Distinct from [ecovoltaics](#term-ecovoltaics), whose ecological ground layer is a function rather than production; the two are the poles of the definitional dispute the lexicon holds open rather than adjudicates (§2.2).

#### Restorative {#term-restorative}

The frame of this entire lexicon rather than a dimension within it. Applied when ecological, hydrological, or economic ground-layer function is a design objective co-equal with generation, not an incidental byproduct. Conventional arrays deliver co-benefits inadvertently or through patchwork policy compliance; *restorative* names the deliberate alternative.

#### Co-location vs. Integration {#term-colocation-integration}

 *Co-location*: panels and a land use share a parcel without functional interdependence. *Integration*: panel height set by livestock clearance, row spacing set by forage light requirements, tracking schedule set by photosynthetic timing. Integration is the line a design crosses to be genuinely restorative, not restorative in name only.

#### Footprint vs. Influence Zone {#term-footprint-influence}

**Footprint**: land physically occupied by racking, panels, access infrastructure. **Influence Zone**: the larger, typically asymmetric area whose hydrology, microclimate, soil, wildlife movement, or visual presence (viewshed) is measurably affected. The solar-siting literature already splits *footprint* the same way — the **array/direct footprint** (panels and racking) versus the **facility/fenceline footprint** (the whole permitted parcel) — and the ecovoltaic siting research makes the distinction matter: several small sites carry higher aggregate edge-to-area ratio than fewer large ones, amplifying both inward effects (pesticide drift) and outward ones (pollination, pest control). **Fragmentation geometry is a first-order design variable.**

Its multi-domain accounting — across Sustainable Communities, Agriculture, Landscapes, and Energy — is the [SCALE footprint](4-restorative-functions.qmd#sec-scale), introduced with the restorative functions (§4).

#### Screening {#term-screening}

The management of the array's outward visual presence: perimeter setbacks, vegetative buffers (hedgerows, tree/shrub belts), earthen berms, fencing treatment, and glint/glare control. It acts on the *visual* portion of the [Influence Zone](#term-footprint-influence). Screening is dual-function — the same vegetative buffer that buys [social license](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures) can carry habitat and connectivity value, so it is pulled by both social license and restorative ambition — while costing generation (edge shade), land, and sometimes agricultural continuity; its habitat value is greatest where the surrounding landscape is otherwise bare of hedgerows. Descriptive only: the lexicon names the lever, not a required buffer width, berm height, or setback.

#### Community Benefit {#term-community-benefit}

The instruments through which a project returns value to its host community: community-benefit or host-community agreements (CBA / HCA), payments in lieu of taxes (PILOT) and tax revenue, good-neighbor / abutter payments, community-solar subscription, local hiring, co-ownership or locally-owned models, and decommissioning bonds as a community-protection instrument. Distinct from acceptance: benefit and acceptance can come apart — benefit without a fair process can read as a bribe — so the [social license](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures) pressure holds both as forces in tension rather than treating a check as consent.

#### Ground Layer {#term-ground-layer}

Whatever occupies the surface beneath and between panels. Primary carrier of restorative function. The solar and agronomic literatures also call this the **understory** or the **ground cover** / **vegetation layer**; "ground layer" is used here because it stays neutral about whether that surface is planted, grazed, gravelled, or bare.

**Syn.:** understory; ground cover; vegetation layer.

#### Marginal / Previously Disturbed Land {#term-marginal-land}

The low-value ground that [idled-land sparing](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions) (S4) presupposes: consistently low-yielding cropland, and previously disturbed land — reclaimed mine land, landfills, and brownfields ("brightfields"). Marginality is partly a property of the ground and partly of the market, so claims of marginal-land siting deserve scrutiny about what fraction of a footprint is genuinely marginal (§2.2).

#### Microclimate Modification {#term-microclimate}

The array's reshaping of the below- and between-panel environment: shade lowers soil and canopy temperature and evaporative demand, raising soil moisture — most in hot, water-limited settings [@barrongafford2019; @sturchio2025; @pinos2026]. Treated as a [restorative function](4-restorative-functions.qmd) (§4.4); itself scale- and geometry-dependent (§1.1).

#### Pore Space {#term-pore-space}

*(borrowed)* — The three-dimensional volume between modules and between modules and ground. Names the thing that "panel height" and "row spacing" only hint at, and treats it as habitat and working room rather than leftover gap.

**Source:** @toledo2021 — [Sources](sources.qmd). Toledo & Scognamiglio's "descriptive model towards a sustainable landscape vision" is a direct predecessor to this lexicon's own describe-the-landscape stance, reading array geometry through landscape-ecology's patch–matrix–corridor lens rather than as a yield problem alone.

#### Ground Coverage Ratio (GCR) {#term-gcr}

The ratio of module area to total ground area — the density of the array. High GCR packs more capacity per acre and pulls with generation yield and capital discipline; low GCR opens the [pore space](#term-pore-space) and inter-row that agrivoltaics and a working ground layer need. GCR is the single number behind much of the row-geometry ↔ ground-layer coupling (§3.3).

#### Module Technology {#term-module-technology}

The panel itself as a lever (§3.3): *monofacial* vs *bifacial* (both faces generate); *vertical bifacial* (east–west, leaving the inter-row open to machinery — extends sharing to larger scale [@vaverkova2026]); *semitransparent / transmissivity-tuned* (passing some light to a crop below); and *spectrally selective* (transmitting the wavelengths plants use while harvesting the rest). Module choice sets how much light — and of what kind — reaches the [ground layer](#term-ground-layer).

#### Tracking Schedule & Curtailment {#term-tracking-curtailment}

Two operational-regime levers (§3.3). *Tracking schedule* — how a single- or dual-axis array is steered through the day, normally to maximize generation, but an ecovoltaic operation may orient panels partly for the light, water, or temperature reaching the ground [@knapp2024]. *Curtailment* — deliberately reducing output for grid, price, or ecological reasons. Both are decisions about how the array is *run* — the instrument of management-led restoration at A4–A5 (§1.4).

#### Land Equivalent Ratio (LER) {#term-ler}

The standard dual-use productivity metric: the land a monoculture would need to match what the co-located system yields on one unit of ground (LER > 1 = a land-productivity gain). It captures *production* co-yield well but is silent on ecological, hydrologic, and community function — it handles the non-production ground layers of [S3–S5](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions) poorly and has no term for the [restorative functions](4-restorative-functions.qmd) or the [SCALE](4-restorative-functions.qmd#sec-scale) domains beyond food and energy. Its blind spots are given alongside it because it is the metric most likely to be taken as the measure of success by default. No single success metric is endorsed here (§8, issue 5).

#### Decommissioning / Repowering / Reversibility {#term-decommissioning}

The end-of-life questions a 25–40-year asset raises: *decommissioning* (removing the array and restoring the ground), *repowering* (replacing modules to extend the site), and *reversibility* (how completely the prior land use can return). Foundation type, soil disturbance, and financial assurance (decommissioning bonds) set how reversible a project is; reversibility is often the crux of the farmland-protection argument, and is itself one of the eight [design pressures](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures) (§3.1).
